name: Reproducible Notebooks and Pipelines
title: Reproducible Notebooks and Pipelines
answer: Reproducible notebooks and pipelines cover the practice of making a quantitative analysis run again and produce the same result, whether on the original machine or another one months later. The scope runs from a single exploratory notebook through to a scheduled pipeline that ingests data, transforms it, fits a model and writes a report. It includes the environment the code runs in, the data it reads, the order in which steps execute, and the record of what was actually run. The aim is that a colleague, a reviewer or the original author can rerun the work and get the same numbers.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Reproducible notebooks and pipelines cover the practice of making a quantitative analysis run again and produce the same result, whether on the original machine or another one months later. The scope runs from a single exploratory notebook through to a scheduled pipeline that ingests data, transforms it, fits a model and writes a report. It includes the environment the code runs in, the data it reads, the order in which steps execute, and the record of what was actually run. The aim is that a colleague, a reviewer or the original author can rerun the work and get the same numbers.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a mix of local machines, shared servers and cloud compute, with notebooks such as Jupyter and pipeline tools such as Airflow, Prefect, Dagster, Snakemake and Make sitting on top. Environment managers like conda, pip with lock files, Docker and similar container tools pin the versions of libraries so a run does not drift when a package updates. Data lives in files, databases or object storage, and version control such as Git tracks the code and sometimes the data or its pointers. Compute may be a laptop, a cluster or a managed service, and the pipeline definition usually has to name which one it expects.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A reproducible setup separates the steps of an analysis into units that can be run in order, with inputs and outputs made explicit rather than hidden in a notebook's memory. Parameters are kept in configuration files or environment variables instead of being edited by hand, and random seeds are fixed so sampling and model fitting repeat. Notebooks are often paired with scripts or parameterised templates so the same logic can run over many inputs without copy and paste. Logs, intermediate outputs and a manifest of versions are kept so a failed or surprising result can be traced back to the exact code, data and settings that produced it. Testing and continuous integration check that the pipeline still runs when something upstream changes.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this area turn on provenance, licensing and the handling of sensitive data. Data sets and code carry licences that govern reuse and redistribution, and a pipeline that pulls from an external source may be bound by terms that change without notice. Personal or confidential data needs access controls, and a reproducible record can itself become a disclosure risk if it captures raw records. Provenance means being able to say where each input came from, who ran what and when, which matters for audit, peer review and internal sign off. Teams often adopt review, retention and access policies so that reproducibility does not conflict with privacy or contractual obligations.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward pipelines that are declared rather than hand run, with environments and data snapshots captured automatically at the moment of execution. Notebook interfaces are converging with pipeline tools, so an exploratory session can be promoted into a scheduled job without a rewrite. Provenance standards and content addressed storage are making it easier to point at an exact version of data and code. The open questions are how much of a run to preserve, how to keep that record usable as tools change, and how to balance reproducibility against the cost of storing every intermediate result.
